title: Focusing on Your Body Can Calm Inflammation, Israeli Researchers Find
excerpt: A preregistered study from Bar-Ilan University found that directing attention toward bodily sensations reduced acute immune responses by 1.5-fold, with roughly 90% of participants showing the effect.
body:
• Directing attention toward bodily sensations produced 1.5-fold smaller inflammatory responses compared to distraction, across three experiments
  • The effect was remarkably consistent, with approximately 90% of participants showing more regulated immune responses under internal attention
  • Two mechanisms were identified: a sensory-dependent pathway and a top-down route engaging the vagus nerve
  • The findings, from Bar-Ilan University in Israel, reframe perception as biologically consequential rather than merely experiential

A new study from Israeli researchers has produced striking evidence that simply paying attention to your body can regulate your immune system. The research, from Bar-Ilan University's Azrieli Faculty of Medicine, found that voluntarily directing attention toward bodily sensations during acute inflammation led to significantly smaller and faster-resolving immune responses — an effect observed in roughly 90% of participants.

The study, authored by Nofar Mizrachi, Rotem Menachem of the Emek Medical Center, and Liron Rozenkrantz of Bar-Ilan University, was posted as a preprint on Research Square in May 2026. It represents one of the first direct demonstrations that voluntary cognitive processes can causally influence acute immune function in humans.

How the Study Worked

Across three preregistered within-subject experiments, researchers used a standardized histamine skin-prick test — a well-characterized method that induces brief, measurable inflammation in the skin. This produces a wheal (swelling) and flare (redness) response that peaks around 15-20 minutes, providing a reliable window to measure immune activity.

Participants underwent the same immune challenge twice under different conditions. In one, they directed their attention internally toward sensations at the inflammation site — the itch, the burning. In the other, they were distracted by external stimuli such as video clips or cognitive tasks. Eye gaze was maintained on a screen throughout, and conditions were counterbalanced to control for order effects.

Striking Results

The results were consistent across all three experiments. When participants focused on their bodily sensations, their inflammatory responses were approximately 1.5-fold smaller than when they were distracted. The wheal response under internal attention measured 3.5 millimeters versus 5.0 millimeters under distraction in the first experiment — a difference the researchers described as "substantial."

Up to 90% of participants across two independent cohorts showed greater inflammation when distracted compared to when paying attention to their body. The effect was not only about magnitude: internal attention also changed the temporal dynamics of the response, with nearly 90% of attentive participants showing stabilization or decline of swelling by the 20-minute mark, compared to just 46% of distracted participants.

"These results establish attention as a cognitive mechanism capable of regulating immune function in vivo."

— Mizrachi, Menachem & Rozenkrantz, Bar-Ilan University

Two Pathways to Immune Regulation

The researchers identified two complementary mechanisms behind the effect. The first is a sensory-dependent route: when participants paid attention to the inflammation site, their perception of sensations like itch and burning was enhanced, and this amplified sensory input appeared to help the body calibrate a more regulated immune response. A third experiment using topical lidocaine to dampen sensory signals confirmed this — reducing sensation weakened, but did not eliminate, the regulatory benefit.

The second pathway is a top-down route engaging the parasympathetic nervous system through vagal activity. The vagus nerve is already known to have anti-inflammatory properties, and the study found evidence that internal attention activated this pathway independently of sensory input.

Connection to Ancient Wellness Traditions

While the study is grounded in rigorous immunology and neuroscience, its implications resonate with practices that have been central to Indian wellness traditions for millennia. Yoga, meditation, and Ayurvedic body-awareness practices all emphasize directing attention inward to bodily sensations — what modern science calls interoception.

The research provides a potential mechanistic explanation for observations long reported by practitioners of these traditions: that mindful body awareness can influence physical health. For the Indian diaspora, which has helped popularize yoga and meditation globally, the findings offer scientific validation of principles embedded in these practices.

What Comes Next

The researchers situated their findings within predictive and allostatic models of brain-body control, arguing that the results "reframe perception as biologically consequential rather than merely experiential." In other words, how you pay attention to your body does not just change how you feel — it changes what your body actually does.

The study is currently a preprint under review and has not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal. If the findings hold up through peer review, they could open new avenues for non-pharmacological approaches to managing inflammatory conditions, from allergies to autoimmune diseases.
